data.title: FDA puts commissioner’s priority voucher framework on ice
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) appears to have quietly paused the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher (CNPV) pilot programme, a controversial expedited review framework established by former agency chief Marty Makary. 

The programme’s shelving was first reported by Reuters, which cited six sources familiar with the matter and internal documents.  

The FDA’s CNPV scheme, which was launched in June 2025, serves as a speedy drug approval process for pharma companies prioritising US interests. It shortens FDA review time for a new drug application from 10-12 months to up to two months. 

Pharma companies needed to demonstrate US-centric potential for the drug to qualify for the programme. The drug would need to address a health crisis in the country, produce an innovative cure for American patients, meet public health needs, or increase domestic drug manufacturing as a national security issue. It marks a stark contrast to existing voucher frameworks used for rare paediatric disease and tropical diseases.  

However, of the 22 drugs given a voucher, slightly more than half were approved. These include MSD’s infertility treatment Pergoveris, Sanofi’s type 1 diabetes drug Tzield (teplizumab), and a gene therapy developed by Regeneron for congenital deafness.  

There was a lack of transparency regarding the programme’s incumbents, however. Analysis by Pharmaceutical Technology identified that a large proportion of the first 15 recipients of a voucher were big pharma companies. Many of these have pricing agreements with the White House.  

Experts interviewed by Pharmaceutical Technology earlier this year questioned the award process. A former FDA reviewer said that the tight approval timelines meant “easy, low-hanging fruit” would be selected over first-in-class drugs with a high profile.  

No new drugs have been equipped with a voucher since Makary’s resignation in May 2026. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary, Robert F Kennedy (RFK) Jr, has previously praised the speed of two approvals granted via the CNPV scheme, though his public comments on the framework have been scarce recently.  

An HHS spokesperson did not immediately respond to Pharmaceutical Technology for comments on the programme’s status, but they have told other outlets that CNPV activities are “ongoing”.  

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard ⁠said that the FDA is reviewing feedback from a June public hearing on it to refine the framework, as per Reuters.

data.title: Neurosterix pockets $105m to advance neuropsychiatry pipeline
data.description:
Swiss biotech company Neurosterix has banked $105m in a Series B funding round to push its range of neuropsychiatric candidates further down the pipeline. 

The financing, which was led by RTW Investments and contributed to by Janus Henderson Investors, GV and Acorn Bioventures – among others – will see Neurosterix progress its range of selective allosteric modulators across various psychiatric conditions.  

The jewel in Neurosterix’s crown is its lead asset, NTX-253 – a brain-penetrant selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator currently in clinical development for schizophrenia. According to the company, indirectly influencing the behaviour of a receptor through allosteric modulation, instead of actively blocking or activating it, can help create differentiated medicines that have a more precise effect. 

With money in the bank, Neurosterix will now progress NTX-253 to Phase II, as the drug has already displayed its potential to act as a once-daily oral treatment in a Phase I single and multiple ascending dose clinical study. 

The biotech sets plans in motion for NTX-253’s debut as Bristol Myers Squibb’s (BMS’s) selective M1 and M4 agonist, Cobenfy (xanomeline and trospium chloride), has started to see increasing clinical uptake in schizophrenia following its US approval in 2024. However, Cobenfy’s launch has had a slow start, with some physicians remaining tentative about prescribing it, while issues with access for American patients via insurance persist. 

Beyond NTX-253, the biotech also has plans for its earlier-stage pipeline, with the company using some of the cash from this raise to progress two other earlier-stage candidates. This includes NTX-819, a metabotropic glutamate receptor 7 (mGlu7)-targeting drug currently in development for mood and anxiety disorders, as well as NTX-529, a second M4-directed therapy, for psychosis and mood-related conditions. 

To help it achieve its goals, Neurosterix is also bolstering its leadership team with a star-studded trio. This will see Andrew Miller and Stephen Brannan, ex-executives at Cobenfy developer and BMS subsidiary, Karuna Therapeutics, join the team – bringing their expertise in neuropsychiatry and muscarinic drugs to the table. 

On top of this, board-certified neurologist and ex-Pfizer leadership member, Endmund Harrigan, will also come on board, bringing his expertise in pharmaceutical development and board leadership. 

According to Miller, muscarinic therapies represent an “important new chapter” in the schizophrenia treatment paradigm, as companies increasingly explore mechanisms outside of the traditional dopamine-based approach. 

“I believe Neurosterix’s highly selective approach to M4 modulation has the opportunity to be an important next-generation muscarinic treatment building on promising early clinical findings,” Miller concluded.

data.title: BMS sets unified research and development structure for 2027
data.description:
Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) is set to merge its separate research and development (R&D) departments into a single entity, effective from 1 January 2027.

The company’s executive vice president and chief medical officer Cristian Massacesi will lead the unified, end-to-end R&D organisation.

The planned structure will place the company’s scientific and clinical expertise within one group, spanning discovery and development.

BMS executive vice president and chief research officer Robert Plenge will remain at the company in an advisory role through March 2027 before departing.

Plenge’s continued involvement is intended to support the transition to the new organisational model.

BMS board chair and CEO Christopher Boerner said: “Bringing Research and Development together as one organisation is an important step in our work to position BMS for long-term growth.

“Under Cristian’s leadership, this new structure will more closely connect our scientific and clinical expertise across R&D, accelerate decision making and ultimately enhance portfolio execution. Increasingly, traditional boundaries between research and development are collapsing.

“This combined R&D organisation sets us up to attract and retain the best talent, build critical capabilities, and better integrate new technology. I want to sincerely thank Robert for his extraordinary and lasting contributions to Bristol Myers Squibb, and his support on evolving the organisation.”

As part of its core operations, BMS works to discover, develop, and deliver medicines intended to help patients address serious diseases.

Massacesi said: “This is an exciting time at BMS, with immense scientific potential and an important opportunity to deliver on the promise of our pipeline while building what comes next. I’m grateful to Robert for his partnership, all he has contributed and the organisation he has built.

“Our Research & Development teams are advancing exceptional science and uniting them as one team will enable us to translate our most promising discoveries into medicines for patients with greater speed and focus.”

data.title: Takeda begins US distribution of narcolepsy type 1 drug Orzeyful
data.description:
Japanese pharma major Takeda has commercially launched Orzeyful (oveporexton) in the US for the treatment for adult patients with narcolepsy type 1.

The therapy is an oral orexin receptor 2 agonist, formulated to target the orexin deficiency that causes the chronic neurological condition.

Following approval by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August 2026, the drug received a Schedule IV controlled substance (CIV) classification.

Distribution across the country is being managed through Accredo Specialty Pharmacy, a division of Evernorth Health Services, with licensed healthcare practitioners able to prescribe the treatment.

Takeda is also offering patient support programmes to assist eligible adults with treatment initiation and healthcare coverage navigation.

Takeda US business unit president Rhonda Pacheco said: “We work for decades toward the defining moments that have the potential to make a real difference for patients.

“Bringing Orzeyful, a first-in-class medicine, to people living with narcolepsy type 1 in the US is one of those moments.

“We’re incredibly proud to be here, and equally focused on what comes next: supporting care and access for patients prescribed Orzeyful.”

Narcolepsy type 1 is described as a rare disorder caused by the loss of orexin-producing neurons. The condition leads to fragmented nocturnal sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness, cognitive difficulties, and cataplexy, which involves sudden and temporary muscle tone loss.

Orzeyful functions by selectively activating orexin receptor 2 pathways to restore signalling, thereby promoting daytime wakefulness and reducing abnormal rapid eye movement sleep phenomena.

In clinical evaluations, the most frequently reported adverse effects included insomnia, excessive saliva production, increased urinary urgency, and urinary frequency.

Regulatory authorities in China and Japan have also approved Orzeyful for adult patients with narcolepsy type 1.

The compound serves as the lead asset in Takeda’s pipeline of orexin-focused treatments.

Alongside Orzeyful, the company is advancing other investigational oral orexin agonists, including TAK-360, which is in clinical development for idiopathic hypersomnia, narcolepsy type 1, and narcolepsy type 2, as well as TAK-495.

Takeda is also creating digital tools and biomarker diagnostic solutions designed to identify and differentiate narcolepsy type 1 earlier.

Jazz Pharmaceuticals’ flagship oxybate blockbuster brands Xywav and Xyrem have traditionally been the top-selling narcolepsy drugs in the US.

data.title: Eli Lilly beats Novo to oral China GLP-1RA market on NMPA approval
data.description:
Eli Lilly has beaten its staunch obesity rival Novo Nordisk to market in China by securing an approval for its weight loss pill orforglipron from the country’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), according to Reuters.

This makes the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), marketed as Foundayo, the first oral drug of its kind to get the regulatory green light in China for use in weight management. 

Before Foundayo’s landmark NMPA blessing, the agency had approved multiple injectable drugs, such as Lilly’s Zepbound (tirzepatide), Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy (semaglutide) and Pfizer & Sciwind Biosciences’ Xianyida (ecnoglutide), as well as Chinese biotech Innovent Biologics’ Xinermei (mazdutide). 

Now that Foundayo has regulatory approval in China, Lilly will expand its use into another geography. The drug is now approved in the US, the United Arab Emirates and the UK, alongside China. This development also puts Lilly ahead of rival obesity player, Novo, which is currently vying for approval of its GLP-1RA pill, oral Wegovy, in China, with the NMPA having accepted its marketing application for the drug earlier this year. Similarly, Huadong Medicine and Jiangsu Hengrui ​Pharmaceuticals are also seeking approvals for their oral weight loss drugs in China. 

While Lilly may be the first to crack the Chinese oral GLP-1RA market, Novo took this title in the US, as it became the first to debut a drug of this type on any global market. Currently, analysts at GlobalData, the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology, forecast that oral Wegovy will take the helm over Foundayo as the best-selling oral GLP-1RA in 2026.  

However, analysts do not foresee the drug holding onto the top-selling spot for long, as they predict that Foundayo will gradually outpace oral Wegovy sales-wise, with the former therapy expected to bring in over $21bn for Lilly in 2032 – significantly eclipsing the $10bn sales predicted for the latter, despite its first-to-market lead. 

Foundayo’s Chinese approval comes as Lilly raised its 2026 outlook for the third time this year after its tirzepatide franchise outperformed several big pharma companies in Q3. Meanwhile, the outlook is not so bright for competitor Novo, as its five-year commercial strategy failed to enamour investors as they raise concerns about the Danish pharma giant’s future growth. 

At the recent 2026 BIO-Europe conference, held in Cologne, Germany, between 9 and 11 November, experts noted that novel targets such as amylin, as well as combinations with GLP-1RAs, will drive the next wave of innovation in the cardiometabolic space, as drugmakers aim to create more tolerable, convenient and muscle-sparing treatment options.

data.title: Blackstone backs Pfizer’s obesity ambitions with $1.5bn fund
data.description:
With an eye on entering the obesity market dominated by Eli Lilly, Pfizer has secured $1.5bn from Blackstone Life Sciences to spur clinical development of its monthly glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) berobenatide.

The private equity firm will bankroll the development costs of berobenatide through 2028. In exchange, Blackstone will be eligible to receive milestone-based payments, dependent on the drug making it to the US market and achieving certain sales figures. The funding does not give Blackstone any ownership rights to berobenatide.

Pfizer is the latest pharma company to tap the financial services of Blackstone. MSD, J&J, and Apogee Therapeutics all have funding arrangements with the equity firm. 

While Pfizer has trimmed parts of its obesity pipeline this year, berobenatide remains front and centre of the drugmaker’s efforts to join the weight loss market. Pfizer acquired the asset – formerly known as MET097i – as part of its $10bn takeover of Metsera in December 2025, a deal that only went through after a fierce bidding war with Novo.

Pfizer has an extensive clinical programme for berobenatide that spans 10 ongoing or planned Phase III studies. Alongside chronic weight management, the asset is also being evaluated for obesity-related comorbidities including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnoea.

Pfizer’s chief financial officer Cecile Guegan said: “Today’s announcement helps us advance our comprehensive obesity programme and maintain the financial capacity and flexibility to invest in our broader pipeline across all therapeutic areas.”

In a research note, Citi analysts said: “The transaction improves the programme’s risk-adjusted economics and enables Pfizer to advance its broad Phase III obesity programme with less near-term financial burden.”

The analysts added that differentiation on efficacy, tolerability and monthly dosing from the late-stage trial remains the key value driver.

The cardiometabolic arena is dominated by Eli Lilly. In Q3, the pharma company’s tirzepatide brands Mounjaro and Zepbound continued their ascendancy. The type 2 diabetes and obesity medications generated $10.7bn and $5.4bn in global sales, respectively.

Tirzepatide’s total quarterly take-home of around $16.1bn meant the drug alone outperformed the total revenue of many other big pharma companies in Q3, including Novartis, GSK, and Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), among others.

While not as dominant as it once was, Novo still occupies significant market share with its semaglutide franchise that now includes a daily pill.  While Novo has raced to market its Wegovy pill in the US, Europe, and the UK first, Lilly is leaning on easier administration of its Foundayo (orforglipron) pill to close the gap. Unlike other territories, Lilly’s pill won approval first in China.

data.title: Beyond GLP-1RA’s: Novel mechanisms and combos to shape future of obesity market
data.description:
In recent years, the emergence of the incretin drug class has revolutionised the cardiometabolic treatment space, as doctors increasingly prescribe weight loss medications for the long-term management of obesity and its associated comorbidities. 

At the epicentre of this movement are pharma giants, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which have made history as of late by commercialising two of the most successful drugs in pharma history – Zepbound/Mounjaro (tirzepatide) and Wegovy/Ozempic (semaglutide). In Q3 2026, tirzepatide sales alone for Lilly were higher than some big pharma company’s entire takings for the quarter, showing the huge demand for these kinds of drugs. 

While these therapies marked the start of the incretin class’s rise to fame, both companies have been battling it out to claim glory with their next-generation therapies – with Lilly’s investigational ‘triple G’ agonist, retatrutide, offering “bariatric surgery-like weight loss efficacy” in recent late-stage trials. 

Now that drugs with strong weight loss efficacy are thriving on the market, many are wondering where the obesity field will go next, as companies look to grab a slice of a segment that a recent GlobalData report estimates will be worth $118.2bn in 2035. 

At a panel session at the 2026 BIO-Europe conference in Cologne, Germany, which took place from 9 to 11 November, experts spoke of a renewed focus in the cardiometabolic space as treatment priorities shift. 

While the segment’s interest has traditionally been on the weight loss efficacy of available therapies, Hamza Bokhari, executive director of preclinical strategy and business development at Swedish biotech Atrogi, noted that people are now looking at the quality of weight loss, as well as the tolerability and durability of effect a therapy can offer.  

Drugmakers are also increasingly focusing on combining incretin therapies with other mechanisms of action (MOAs), such as amylin-based therapies, which Willem Broekaert, managing partner at V-Bio Ventures, mentioned could help address unmet needs in groups such as treatment non-responders. 

Meanwhile, Hellmut Augustin, DVM, PhD, director of the Helmholtz Institute for Translational AngioCardioScience, tells Pharmaceutical Technology that the cardiometabolic space would likely benefit from targeting adipose tissue directly, as finding therapies to protect organs impacted by complications of cardiometabolic disease could represent a positive step forward. 

“Mitochondrial function is one of the major targets,” Augustin said, adding that energy expenditure and lipolysis could also be fruitful areas for development.   

Considering best practices for running cardiometabolic trials 

During the panel session, experts were also keen to talk about cardiometabolic clinical trials, which can face notable challenges from patient retention to determining suitable endpoints. 

One hurdle that Olivia Cavlan, partner at LifeArc, a British self-funded medical research organisation, pointed to was trying to design a proof-of-concept endpoint for trials to measure functional benefit when testing a muscle-sparing therapy in the context of obesity treatment.  

According to Bokhari, this requires a sponsor to determine what they mean by muscle function – whether that be discussing power, strength endurance or a composite score, and there is currently no consensus agreement on which is the best to use.  

Outside of this, Philip Brainin, CEO of IsoMab, a UK biotech, noted that it may be time to question if cardiovascular outcome trials are always needed. “I see regulators becoming more patient-centric as a trend,” he commented, adding that quality of life matters more now than ever. To back this up, he highlights the US approval of Bristol Myers Squibb’s (BMS) Camzyos (mavacamten) in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy based on measures of exercise capacity in a non-outcome trial. 

“You can come at this in a symptom-driven way,” Brainin commented, adding that if a drug produces symptoms that are meaningful to patients, then it’s possible that a company can run a pre-concept trial with less than 200 patients in six months, rather than the years it may take to run an outcomes trial. 

This, Brainin said, would likely be more doable when liaising with the cardiorenal division of the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which he says is “more open for discussions” than the divisions in charge of obesity and diabetes, which generally only accepts body weight reductions over changes like shifts in body composition. 

However, Brainin stressed that this was not him wanting to get rid of outcomes studies, as he believes they would be highly beneficial in the post-marketing setting. “Biotechs can push regulatory interactions; dare to ask questions, but with a data-driven approach,” Brainin concluded.

data.title: Podcast: Longevity, China, and AI the talk of the town at BIO Europe 2026
data.description:
With the curtains closing on another year at BIO-Europe, the attending editorial team is still revelling in the interesting conversations from the conference, as patrons gathered to chat about where the industry will go in 2027 as this year comes to a close.  

In this episode of the GlobalData Healthcare Podcast, reporters Jam Bensilum and Annabel Kartal-Allen outline the key takeaways while reporting on the ground at the 2026 BIO-Europe conference, held in Cologne, Germany from 9-11 November.  

Specifically, they delve into topics including China’s rising influence, artificial intelligence (AI), Europe’s competitiveness, and the latest developments in emerging therapeutic areas. 

Kartal-Allen also chats with Cedric Moreau, partner at prominent European venture capital firm, Sofinnova Partners, about what he thinks will be big in M&A going into 2027, and what impact the US midterms will have on the sector moving forward. 

With conference season in full swing, keep an eye out for podcasts covering the key takeaways from big events like the upcoming London Life Sciences week. 

In addition, you can find plenty of other episodes, bringing you the latest insights into the wonderful world of pharma, biotech, medtech and clinical trials at this link.

data.title: Life-extending peptides are likely not around the corner
data.description:
Excitement in the longevity space over peptides comes with the caveat that many claims about their life-extending potential are incomplete at best and unfounded at worst.

Interest around longevity research emerged across several talks on the opening day of the Financial Times’ 2026 Global Pharma and Biotech Summit held in London, UK, 10–11 November. During a dedicated panel on longevity therapeutics, experts agreed that though there are promising signs with peptides, data around their effects on lifespan are not yet conclusive, while in many cases claims of efficacy are largely unfounded.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) have shown signs of age reversal by some metrics, according to Alex Zhavoronkov, CEO of Insilico Medicine. For example, proteomics data published in September 2026 by researchers from Novo and Harvard University found Novo’s GLP-1RA semaglutide reduced biological age by as much as four years in the heart, brain, lungs, and other organs. Semaglutide is marketed as Wegovy for treating obesity.

However, Zhavoronkov added that such data hasn’t been backed by conclusive mortality data showing an overall increased lifespan with GLP-1RAs. Such studies need to be large-scale and long-term to capture any benefit, which will take a long time to prove, he said.

Tim Spector, a professor of genetic epidemiology at King’s College London, UK, and a fixture in the online health space, said GLP-1RAs have been the biggest medical breakthrough he’s seen during his career. But the idea of these being miracle drugs for longevity is misguided, he added.

He in turn touted the potential of the gut microbiome as a predictor for future health. According to patient data tracked by ZOE, a health company Spector co-founded, GLP-1RA users often have poor gut health. A causative relationship has been suggested by some, but these drugs’ effects are still not fully understood.

In lieu of solid longevity data, unsubstantiated claims and misinformation have crept in. Zhavoronkov described “snake oil statements” being made about supposedly life-extending drugs like peptides. The issue is perpetuated by social media, according to Tina Vilsbøll, senior medical officer at Novo, who warned, “there is no quick fix in this area.”

The longevity space is also fraught with issues around trust. Greg Bailey, co-founder of Juvenescence, an aging-focused biotech, said companies developing longevity drugs will need to gain credibility and authenticity in the eyes of patients, particularly as a counter to the surprising uptake of untested peptides for longevity which he has seen.

Although, he noted that explaining clinical nuance to a mass audience could complicate attempts to gain trust. To counter this, Bailey’s company is employing celebrity advocates to reach patients.

data.title: FDA and EMA waive paediatric studies for Shanton’s gout candidate
data.description:
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have granted paediatric clinical trial waivers to Shanton Pharma for its lead candidate SAP-001, easing the drug’s regulatory paths to approval.

Under an agreement reached with the EMA on a paediatric investigation plan (PIP), the clinical-stage biotechnology company received a full, product-specific waiver.

The decision applies across all paediatric age groups diagnosed with hyperuricemia, except for conditions arising from obesity or chronic kidney disease.

The European determination follows an agreed initial paediatric study plan (PSP) submitted in May of this year to the FDA.

Regulators at the FDA similarly exempted SAP-001 from paediatric study requirements because gout occurs with extremely low frequency in children.

Shanton Pharma CEO Bing Li said: “We are pleased that the EMA and FDA have determined that paediatric clinical studies evaluating SAP-001 are not needed to support market authorisation applications for hyperuricemia and gout.

“The EMA and FDA waivers significantly lessen the administrative and regulatory burden and lower the overall cost of clinical development of SAP-001.”

SAP-001 is an investigational, once-daily oral urate-lowering therapy designed to treat uncontrolled and refractory gout in adult patients.

In a recent Phase IIb study (NCT05690204), the compound demonstrated efficacy and safety in individuals whose hyperuricemia failed to respond to standard-of-care xanthine oxidase inhibitor treatments.

Last year, the FDA granted fast track designation (FTD) to the drug candidate, supported in part by the Phase IIb results indicating its potential to improve upon existing urate-lowering therapies for patients facing unmet medical needs.

Established in 2016 by pharmaceutical entrepreneurs, Shanton Pharma is a privately held business focused on developing treatments for adults with gout and hyperuricemia.

The company maintains its corporate headquarters in Singapore, alongside research and development activities based in China, Singapore, and the US.
